new_statements.quote: The pitch pattern in disyllabic words is like a template. Each syllable must fit into the template regardless of its characteristics in citation form (or underlying form). The non-initial syllable carries high pitch, with no designation for register. Similarly, it does not carry any designation for level/falling. It is always high falling. In transcribing disyllabic words, I find that a helpful auditory clue is listening for a perceived stress on the second syllable (high register) and a jump up in pitch to the second syllable (low register). By following these two clues, I can accurately note which of the two patterns the word belongs to.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dolpo Tibetan is analysed as a word-tone ('tone template') language, not a stress language: the register (high vs low) of the first syllable is the only contrastive prosodic feature of a (di)syllabic word; the non-initial syllable is always high-falling (55-52 / 24-52 patterns), and the tonal domain does not exceed two syllables. The author does not state a stress rule; he reports only that, auditorily, the second syllable of a high-register disyllable sounds stressed and that low-register disyllables have a pitch jump up to the second syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: p.34 describes the second syllable of [the we] 'dust' (high-register-initial) as 'unstressed', which sits uneasily with the p.35 remark; the monosyllabic length-pitch correlation (long = level, short = falling) does not hold in polysyllables; second syllables can be contrastively long via morphology (p.18-19). Trisyllabic and quadrisyllabic compounds split into separate tonal domains (sec. 6.1.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word up to two syllables (disyllabic template); compounds of 3-4 syllables pattern as 1+2 or 2+2 tonal domains. Data are citation forms recorded for acoustic analysis; variety: 'Dolpo Tibetan.. spoken in Dolpo district of West Nepal' (no village named). Section heading groups Dolpo with Mugom Tibetan but the pitch traces and tables are Dolpo.
new_statements.identity_note: Watters 2002 describes 'Dolpo Tibetan.. spoken in Dolpo district of West Nepal' (no village given) and heads the section 'Dolpo Tibetan (and Mugom)', claiming Mugom Tibetan (Mugu village; Glottolog Mugom-Karmarong mugo1238) shares the same tone-template system, but all Dolpo figures/tables are Dolpo data. Kopp's data are from the Nangkhong (Nangkong) valley; Hojer Lama 2017 and Tournadre & Suzuki list four valleys (Tsharka, Tarap, Panzang, Nangkhong). Tichyurong (Honda 2018) is a neighbouring, separately listed variety and is not covered here. All map to dolp1239.

sources.note: Acoustic tone study. Dolpo Tibetan (sec. 6.1.2-6.1.3, pp.33-37; summary p.44, 48) is a 'tone template' word-tone language: 4-way pitch contrast on monosyllables reduces to two disyllabic patterns determined by the register of the first syllable; the non-initial syllable is always high falling regardless of its citation form; tonal domain is at most two syllables (compounds split into pairs). Stress is mentioned only incidentally: p.35 'a helpful auditory clue is listening for a perceived stress on the second syllable (high register) and a jump up in pitch to the second syllable (low register)…
